name: Jade Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers or AI companies. This is confidential. What's an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach piano before lunch, then rehearse viola with the quartet or edit a student's audition tape. The music is lovely when four of us lock in, but I'm always chasing a late fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did the last month look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A wedding deposit slipped and I covered rent with lesson money. My master's in music helps me teach, but there aren't many similar jobs nearby.

say: I'd say **live music** still brings listeners into a room.
I'd welcome **faster bookings** because email work takes time from practice.
think: My **rent** is at risk already, even if AI barely changes anything.
The **six pupils** give me steadier money than wedding shows.
do: Keep my **six pupils** on their weekly lesson slots.
Put **thirty per show** into a rent account whenever a fee clears.
feel: I feel **Relieved** about the stage, but anxious over the next booking gap.
S0.quote: A good reputation doesn't pay the rent between weddings.
fieldNote: Her **public confidence** in live music hides less than a month's savings.
The **late wedding deposit** shows why ordinary uncertainty already threatens her rent and limits her choices.

steps.text: Keep six pupils on weekly lesson slots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet the Friday audience still pays to hear people in a room. A faster booking email won't play the viola for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already worried about rent, quite apart from AI. I have less than a month's expenses saved, and the wedding deposit that was late last month nearly wrecked me. A good reputation doesn't pay the rent between weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep six pupils on their weekly slots and ask the venue manager for two winter dates this week. If those shows pay, I'll move thirty from each fee to a rent account during the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm glad the stage still needs us. The gap between bookings still makes me wake at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much room do you have if a show falls through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding moved last February and I borrowed from my sister to cover the studio. I paid her back, but there was nothing left for another cancellation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your week would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the school first if I had to move a lesson. Those six pupils pay every week, and the venues don't.

I'd say **live shows** still need players, even with generated demos.
think: The **editing fees** could vanish before my stage work does.
Fewer **lesson hours** would hurt my rent more than a clever music demo.

Offer a **group class** only if the school lends a room and eight pupils enrol.
feel: I feel **Squeezed** by lost hours, though I can change how I teach.
S1.quote: I can't live on applause if the hours around the stage disappear.
fieldNote: She separates **live performance** from editing and lesson tasks exposed to thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet to check our recording rights before sending clients files. I think clients will start bringing machine-made demos to rehearsal, but they'll still need players for a live show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small arranging and editing jobs could vanish first, and I use those to fill the gaps. The school might use automated practice feedback and reduce my lesson hours, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the school for confirmed spring hours and try the AI practice tool a colleague has tested. In the first year of the shift, I'll offer a group rehearsal class if the school lends me a room and eight pupils sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel squeezed because the stage can survive while the hours around it disappear. I can change a lesson, but I can't live on applause if the hours around the stage disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paid task could go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of my nine paid teaching hours are really editing audition tapes. Losing those would take nearly a whole rent payment over a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a practice tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't give a pupil a shortcut I haven't tried myself. If my colleague's pupils still hear their own mistakes after using the AI tool, I'll test it with mine.

I'd admit **cheap scores** might undercut our paid arranging immediately.

feel: I feel **Alarmed** by rent and the short warning before teaching income might shrink.
S2.quote: My live shows might survive until robots arrive, but the supporting income may not.
fieldNote: The **2028 deadline** gives her little savings runway to replace teaching pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At rehearsal I'd tell everyone to keep playing and keep the rights to our recordings. I wouldn't promise them all will be fine when clients can get a complete score in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a system could compose, arrange and coach better and cheaper than I can. A live audience might still hire me, but losing lessons and editing would empty the calendar before robot players arrive around 2031. My live shows might survive until robots arrive, but the supporting income may not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total last quarter's pay by source and ask the venue for a six-month residency. If lessons drop below six a week during the first year after 2028, I'll take café shifts; if that doesn't cover rent, I'll end the separate studio rental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I can picture the rent letter and no spare month behind it. I still want to make music, but wanting it isn't a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense would go first if lessons collapsed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio costs about four hundred a month and renews monthly. I could teach at the school if the head agrees, but I haven't asked yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could you get replacement pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The café by the station offered weekend cover before. I'd call again only if lesson numbers fell, because teaching is still the job I want.

I'd tell students their **music degree** can still help while audiences decide what they want.
think: **AGI in 2031** could remove composing fees before robot players arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to build an audience that asks for this quartet by name. I wouldn't tell music students their degree is useless before we know what customers choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take the composing fees, but I could make teaching less about marking exercises. Robot players around 2034 might reach routine events; I think weddings could still want humans, though I can't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll run one paid chamber workshop next term, then each term if it pays in a borrowed school room. By 2031 I'll seek a year's teaching and venue contracts, and in the first year after AGI I'll replace editing hours with ensemble teaching if enough pupils sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less cornered than with two years. Five years lets me test a workshop; it doesn't put five months of rent in my account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first workshop cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd charge each pupil a small fee and borrow the room rather than take another lease. If fewer than eight enrol, I'd stop after one term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the first term fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite my quartet to coach if the first class pays its way. If it fails, I'd keep six regular pupils and ask for more venue dates.

I'd say a **ten-year runway** gives musicians time to find paying audiences.

S4.quote: I cannot buy a future with an empty room today.
fieldNote: She uses ten years to build **live community** work without ignoring current rent.
Her **insurance and ticket** conditions keep the chamber evenings affordable while she still relies on weekly lessons for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to choose what sort of musician I want to be. I'd still tell pupils to learn to listen, not merely produce a tidy file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 37 when full AGI arrives in 2036, so retirement isn't an escape. Cheap arranging and feedback could hurt me, and robot performers around 2039 could take some venue work; human company would have to earn its fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn I'll try two chamber evenings in the library hall if ticket sales cover the players and insurance. Over the decade I'll build a cash reserve from classes and shows; in the first year after 2036 I'll keep the evenings only if the books still balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm more hopeful because there is time to try something small. Today's rent is still due, so a decade only helps if the first experiment is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a chamber night affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library hall is free for community evenings, but they want insurance. I'll ask the quartet to split that cost before announcing any date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How quickly would you expand it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't expand beyond two evenings until seats sell. I cannot buy a future with an empty room today.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because lessons and arranging could shrink before I've saved even one month's rent. A six-month venue contract and affordable school room for teaching would give me somewhere to stand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns a recording when a client sends an AI-made demo. I want that written down before my quartet signs away a performance we spent weeks making.

headlineQuote: I still want to make music, but wanting it isn't a budget.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** musician with a master's degree who teaches, edits tapes and plays viola in a quartet.
Her **thin savings** make gaps between weddings and weekly lessons frightening even in AI Plateau.
She sees **thinking AI** threatening arranging and teaching income before robots reach live performance three years later.
She tests **workshops and chamber nights** with borrowed rooms, enough pupils or ticket sales, and no new lease.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because cheap composing and feedback could cut income before she has a rent reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A **six-month venue contract** and affordable school room would protect live and teaching work while she adjusts.
